segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he saw the crowds, he went up the mountain, and after he sat down, his disciples came to him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he opened his mouth and began to teach them, saying:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of the heavens.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Blessed are the gentle, for they will inherit the earth.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be satisfied.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Blessed are the merciful, for they will be shown mercy.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Blessed are those who have been persecuted for the sake of righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of the heavens.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Blessed are you when people insult you and persecute you and falsely say every kind of evil against you because of me.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in the heavens; for that is how they persecuted the prophets who came before you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt loses its taste, with what will it be salted? It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled underfoot by people.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: You are the light of the world. A city set on top of a mountain cannot be hidden.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Nor do people light a lamp and put it under the measuring basket, but on the lampstand, and it shines for everyone in the house.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: In the same way, let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father in the heavens.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish but to fulfill.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For truly I tell you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota, not one stroke of a letter, will pass away from the Law until everything has taken place.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So whoever sets aside one of the least of these commandments and teaches people to do the same will be called least in the kingdom of the heavens; but whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of the heavens.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For I tell you that unless your righteousness goes far beyond that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of the heavens.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: You have heard that it was said to the people of old, ‘You shall not murder, and whoever murders will be liable to judgment.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But I tell you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment; and whoever says to his brother, ‘Raka,’ will be liable to the council; and whoever says, ‘Fool!’ will be liable to the Gehenna of fire.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: leave your gift there in front of the altar and go. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Come to terms quickly with your opponent at law while you are with him on the road, or your opponent may hand you over to the judge, and the judge to the officer, and you will be thrown into prison.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Truly I tell you, you will never get out of there until you have paid back the last penny.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But I tell you that everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you; for it is better for you to lose one of your members than for your whole body to be thrown into Gehenna.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And if your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you; for it is better for you to lose one of your members than for your whole body to go off into Gehenna.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: It was also said, ‘Whoever divorces his wife must give her a certificate of divorce.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But I tell you that everyone who divorces his wife, except on the ground of sexual immorality, makes her commit adultery, and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Again, you have heard that it was said to the people of old, ‘You shall not break an oath, but shall fulfill your oaths to the Lord.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But I tell you, do not swear at all: neither by heaven, for it is God’s throne;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: nor by the earth, for it is the footstool of his feet; nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And do not swear by your head, for you cannot make one hair white or black.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Let your word be ‘Yes, yes’ or ‘No, no’; anything more than these comes from the evil one.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But I tell you, do not resist the one who is evil. Instead, whoever slaps you on the right cheek, turn the other to him as well;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and if anyone wants to sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and whoever presses you into service for one mile, go with him two.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Give to the one who asks you, and do not turn away from the one who wants to borrow from you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But I tell you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: so that you may become children of your Father in the heavens; for he makes his sun rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And if you greet only your brothers, what more are you doing? Do not even the Gentiles do the same?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So you are to be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.”

notes.note: Matthew's Greek has the plural, “the heavens,” reflecting the Hebrew and Aramaic word for heaven, which is always plural. Most English versions flatten it to “heaven.” The plural is kept here, and in “your Father in the heavens,” because a first-century hearer would have recognized it as a Semitic turn of phrase.

“Meek” now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes someone gentle, humble and not self-assertive, and “gentle” or “humble” is the usual modern rendering. The verse echoes Psalm 37:11, where the same Greek word in the Septuagint stands for the humble poor who will inherit “the land”; the Greek word translated “earth” here can mean either.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice, justify. The word covers both being in the right before God and doing what is right. Translations into most other languages use their word for “justice” throughout, and some scholars prefer “justice” in English as well.

The Greek verb ordinarily means “become foolish” or “make foolish.” Here and in Luke 14:34 it is used of salt that has become insipid and useless. A Greek hearer may well have caught the double sense, a warning against disciples who become fools; some scholars suggest an underlying Aramaic wordplay, but that is uncertain.

notes.phrase: not one iota, not one stroke of a letter
notes.note: Iota is the smallest letter of the Greek alphabet and here stands for yod, the smallest Hebrew letter. The “stroke” (literally “little horn”) is a small mark or projection on a letter; exactly which feature of the script is meant is debated. The point is that not even the smallest detail of the Law will lapse.

notes.traditional: angry with his brother without a cause
notes.note: Many manuscripts add “without cause” after “brother,” and the King James Version follows them. The words are absent from several of the earliest witnesses, and most editors judge them an early addition meant to soften the saying. The shorter text is translated here.

Matthew leaves this Aramaic insult untranslated in his Greek, so it is left as it stands here. It is a term of contempt, probably meaning something like “empty-head.” The “council” is a judicial body; the word is also used for the high council in Jerusalem, the Sanhedrin.

Gehenna is a place name, the Valley of Hinnom beside Jerusalem, which the prophets associated with child sacrifice and coming judgment and which by the first century had become a name for the place of final punishment. Many translations render it “hell,” usually with a footnote giving the name. The name is kept here because “hell” merges it with Hades, a different word, and with later imagery.

The Greek expresses purpose: looking with the aim of desiring. The verb is the one the Septuagint uses in the commandment “You shall not covet your neighbor's wife,” and the word for “woman” can also mean “wife,” so the saying may have another man's wife specifically in view. Most translations render “lustfully” or “with lust,” which can suggest that any passing attraction is meant.

The verb comes from the Septuagint's word for a trap or obstacle and means to trip someone up so that they fall away from loyalty to God. The King James “offend” now suggests hurt feelings, which is too weak. Modern versions divide between “cause to stumble” and “cause to sin”; the first is used here because it keeps the picture and is not limited to a single act of sin.

notes.phrase: except on the ground of sexual immorality
notes.traditional: saving for the cause of fornication
notes.note: The Greek word is a broad term for unlawful sexual intercourse of any kind. Most interpreters take it here to mean sexual unfaithfulness by the wife. Others have argued for a narrower reference, such as marriages within the degrees of kinship forbidden in Leviticus 18 or unchastity before marriage; the question remains disputed.

The Greek form can be masculine (“the evil person”) or neuter (“evil”). The examples that follow, a slap, a lawsuit, a forced march, point to a person who does wrong to you. Some scholars also argue that “resist” here means specifically to retaliate by force or in court. The same form in verse 37 is rendered “the evil one,” meaning the devil, though “evil” is possible there as well.

The verb is a technical term, Persian in origin, for the right of officials and soldiers to requisition civilians and their animals to carry loads. The same word is used when Simon of Cyrene is made to carry the cross in Matthew 27:32. Hearers in Roman-occupied Galilee would have known the practice at first hand.

“Love your neighbor” is from Leviticus 19:18, but “hate your enemy” is not found in Scripture. It appears to summarize a common inference that the command to love applied only to one's own people. Comparable language about hating outsiders is found in the Dead Sea Scrolls.

notes.phrase: pray for those who persecute you
notes.traditional: bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you
notes.note: Many later manuscripts have a longer form of this verse, adding blessing those who curse you and doing good to those who hate you. The additions appear to have been brought in from the parallel in Luke 6:27–28. The earliest manuscripts have the shorter text translated here.

The Greek word means complete, whole or fully grown, and in the Septuagint it renders the Hebrew for being wholehearted or blameless before God (for example Deuteronomy 18:13). In context it describes love that is undivided, extending to enemies as God's does, more than moral flawlessness in the abstract. “Perfect” is kept because the comparison is with God, but “complete” or “whole” are defensible renderings.

candidates.reason: Recurs throughout the New Testament for fellow members of the community regardless of sex, and translators divide between “brother,” “brother or sister” and “fellow believer.”
